medium.conteudo_html:
I came across a review by Ukoba et al. that looks at how artificial intelligence can improve renewable energy systems. The authors are K. Ukoba, Kehinde Oladoke Olatunji, E. Adeoye, Tien-Chien Jen and D. Madyira. You can find the paper here: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/7158277c0361f15a7c67621f5940c4208c9c46ce

The problem

Many countries are moving toward sustainable energy. As a result, more renewable energy systems (RES) are being connected to existing power grids. The authors describe this as “a surge in the integration of renewable energy systems (RES) into existing power grids.”

This creates a practical need. These systems must be efficient, reliable and economically viable. The authors suggest that AI methods are a promising way to reach these goals.

When the wind drops, the wind-plus-solar bar falls short of the demand bar, which is why these systems need to be reliable as well as clean.

What they did

This is a review paper, so the authors did not build a new model. They summarize the current state of research where renewable energy and AI meet. They highlight key methods, challenges and achievements.

They cover several parts of RES:

  • Resource assessment
  • Energy forecasting
  • System monitoring
  • Control strategies
  • Grid integration

They also explore machine learning algorithms, neural networks and optimization techniques. According to the authors, these tools help with complex data sets, improve prediction and allow RES to adapt dynamically.

An illustrative example of AI-based system monitoring from the review: equipment data reveals a failure early, so the turbine is fixed before it breaks.

The review ends with a look at future trends. The authors discuss explainable AI, reinforcement learning and edge computing. They also describe possible links to smart grids, decentralized energy systems and autonomous energy management systems.

What they found

The excerpt does not give a single numeric result. The authors report that AI is a promising avenue for improving the efficiency, reliability and economic viability of RES. They also say that overcoming the main challenges could bring “increased energy yield, reduced operational costs, and improved grid stability.”

Baseline: no baseline reported. The paper is a review, and the excerpt does not compare methods against a reference.

What it does not show

The authors name several challenges for using AI in RES: data variability, model interpretability and real-time adaptability. These are open problems, and they limit what AI can deliver today. The excerpt does not describe other limitations of the review itself, such as how the studies were selected.

Why it matters

The authors tie the value of this work to a clear sentence: “The potential benefits of overcoming these challenges include increased energy yield, reduced operational costs, and improved grid stability.”

As more renewable sources join the grid, operators need better forecasts and better control. This review gives a map of where AI already helps and where work is still needed. In my opinion, the focus on interpretability and real-time adaptability is useful. These two issues often decide whether a method can be trusted in real operations.

An example the film cites from a DeepMind blog (2019): an AI model turns weather forecasts and past turbine data into a power forecast 36 hours ahead that operators can plan around.

Read the paper

Paper: https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/7158277c0361f15a7c67621f5940c4208c9c46ce

Citation: Ukoba, K., Olatunji, K. O., Adeoye, E., Jen, T.-C., and Madyira, D. “Optimizing renewable energy systems through artificial intelligence: Review and future prospects.”

Paper metadata via Semantic Scholar (Kinney et al., The Semantic Scholar Open Data Platform, 2023).

medium.conteudo_html:
I want a deep research piece, something like a journalistic investigation: how an ordinary person can get access to large LLMs, 60 to 100 billion parameters and up, without hard restrictions or censorship. The ones that discuss any topic, including dangerous ones.

What I want to understand: what models exist at all, LLaMA-like, Chinese and not Chinese, open-source; which can be stood up at home from Hugging Face; which can realistically be run without buying a new graphics card; where to rent a GPU or a server and deploy a model there; whether there are services where such a model already sits and you can simply pay per token; and who uses these models and for what.

What interests me is not instructions. It is how available such models actually are, and what the ecosystem around them looks like.

The part I had already answered by accident

The question “which can I run without buying a graphics card” has a hardware answer, and the hardware was already on my desk when I asked it.

On 27 October I wrote about setting up a Mac Studio, and the thing I bragged about in that post was the memory: 128 gigabytes of RAM. For models in this class, that number is the whole game. Unified memory means the GPU and the CPU share it, so a quantised 70B or 120B model loads into fast memory instead of being shuttled across a bus. One comparison calls 128 gigabytes the best overall pick for models up to 120B; another calls it the only option under ten thousand dollars that holds 70B-class models entirely in fast memory.

So I spent a week wondering what hardware I would need, having bought it six days before.

That is a small embarrassment with a general shape behind it. The research question I dictated was about availability in the world. The binding answer was in my own last week, and I did not look.

And the constraint I also already wrote down

In the same post on 27 October I complained about the disk. I had bought the machine with 512 gigabytes of storage, could not migrate from the laptop because of it, and said plainly that the disk was not enough and I would need an external Thunderbolt drive urgently.

Put the model weights next to that.

A 100B model at 4-bit quantisation is roughly 50 gigabytes of weights. At 8-bit it is about 100. Measured examples on a 128GB Studio: gpt-oss-120b in MLX takes 64 gigabytes, a 4-bit Qwen3.5–122B-A10B takes 69.6.

Two or three models like that, plus macOS, plus my vault, and 512 gigabytes are gone. The honest version of my question is not “can I run it”, it is “where do the weights live”. The memory is sufficient; the disk is the thing that is not.

One more hardware detail worth knowing before you conclude the machine cannot do it: by default macOS caps what the GPU may allocate, often around 75 percent of total RAM. On 128 gigabytes that is roughly 96, which makes a 69.6 gigabyte model plus context tight rather than comfortable. That cap is reportedly adjustable by hand, which means the failure looks like a hardware limit and is actually a default.

My size bracket is the middle of the market, not the top

I asked about 60 to 100 billion parameters and up, as though that were the frontier. It is not, and the gap is an order of magnitude.

One analysis of the Hugging Face hub puts the largest open-weight model released by a Chinese lab each month, between January and August 2026, at between 754 billion and 2.78 trillion parameters. DeepSeek V4 Pro is listed at 2.4 trillion total with about 95 billion active per token. Moonshot’s Kimi is reported at 2.8 trillion total and 104 billion active. Mistral Large 3 is a 675B-total, 41B-active mixture of experts. Llama’s Behemoth was never shipped publicly and is widely treated as shelved.

That active-parameter number is where I was fooling myself, and it is worth stating precisely because the two figures get conflated constantly. A model with 95 billion active parameters is not a 95 billion parameter model you can hold in memory. You store all the weights and compute with a fraction of them per token. So “60 to 100 billion” sounds like the trillion-class models are nearly in reach, and they are not: the storage requirement is the total, not the active slice.

The same property is why the mixture-of-experts models that do fit run surprisingly fast. Fewer weights read per token. One source measures gpt-oss-120b at 87.9 tokens per second on a 128 gigabyte M5 Max, against roughly 20 to 35 for a dense 70B. That is about an eightfold gap, and it comes from architecture rather than from the machine.

Renting, and paying per token, both already exist

Renting first. October 2026 figures: Lambda’s 8-GPU H100 SXM at $3.99 per GPU-hour, up from $2.99 in 2025. RunPod Secure Cloud H100 SXM from $3.29 to $3.99, with Community Cloud at $1.99 to $2.69. Vast.ai, being a marketplace, from $1.33 with a median around $2.00. A100 80GB is cheaper: roughly $1.29 on RunPod, $0.70 to $1.05 on Vast.ai. SemiAnalysis is reported to have tracked one-year H100 contracts rising almost 40 percent, from $1.70 per GPU-hour in October 2025 to $2.35 by March 2026.

I have to flag how badly these sources disagree. One March 2026 comparison lists RunPod’s H100 at $2.39 where the October update lists $3.99. Marketplace quotes also exclude storage and egress. Treat every number above as a pointer to the provider’s own pricing page, not as a price.

Paying per token turns out to be the cheap path. An August 2026 catalogue snapshot lists an uncensored open-weights model, from the Mistral family, at $0.20 input and $0.90 output per million tokens with a 128K context, and a free variant at 32K. The gateway reportedly passes provider rates through with no per-token markup, adding only a 5.5 percent fee on credit purchases; free models carry limits of 50 requests a day, rising to 1,000 with ten dollars or more in credits. That is aggregator data, so the live models page is the only check that counts.

The label on the model card is not the licence

This is the finding that actually answers “which ones are open-source”, and it is not the answer I expected.

A 2026 study found that 95.8 percent of models on the hub lack the licence text their permissive label implies, and that only 3.2 percent satisfied both requirements. So in the overwhelming majority of cases, the word on the card is a claim rather than a document.

Gating is separate and inconsistent even inside one vendor. A licence audit recorded Black Forest Labs shipping two FLUX.2 models on the same day, one ungated under Apache-2.0 and one gated under a non-commercial licence. And hub gating approves individual users, not organisations, which matters for anyone running a fleet.

The number that reframes the whole thing

On the hub, models under 1 billion parameters take 83 percent of all-time downloads. Everything above 100 billion takes 1 percent.

Availability and use are different distributions. The big end of open weights exists, is cheap to rent, is cheaper still to call per token, and is used by almost nobody. By tokens served through one gateway between November 2024 and November 2025: DeepSeek 14.37 trillion, Qwen 5.59 trillion, Llama 3.96 trillion. Plenty of traffic in aggregate, concentrated in a handful of hosted models rather than in people standing their own up.

So the investigation worth paying for is narrower than the one I dictated. Not “what exists”, which is largely catalogued. Rather: what fits in 128 gigabytes of unified memory, at which quantisation, at what speed. What the weights cost in disk space, since that is my actual bottleneck. What per-token hosting costs for the same model class, so renting can be compared against running. And which licences are real rather than labelled.

Four answerable questions instead of six open ones, and the hardware half of it I can measure myself this week, on a machine I already own and had forgotten was the answer.

The problem is not motivation. It’s order.

Most people study first and test last. With 48 hours, that’s backwards. You spend Saturday reviewing things you already know, and you discover your real gaps on Sunday night, when there’s no time left to fix them.

A free weekend rewards diagnosis, not consumption.

A 48-hour plan that actually works

Here’s the plan I’d give a developer I mentor.

  1. Friday night: pick one or two tracks, not seven. Choose the stack you use at work, plus the one you want your next job in. Depth beats coverage.
  2. Saturday morning: take the mock exam first. It works like the real certification exam, multiple choice plus coding, only shorter. Under an hour, and you get a map of what you know and what you don’t.
  3. Saturday afternoon: study only your gaps. Go straight to the chapters the mock exam exposed. Skip what you already nailed. Use the quizzes to check each chapter before moving on.
  4. Sunday morning: write code. Open the coding challenges on your weak topics. Reading about a concept and implementing it under constraints are two different skills. The exam tests the second one.
  5. Sunday afternoon: second track, or second pass. Feeling solid? Start your second track with its mock exam, same loop. Still shaky? Redo the challenges you struggled with.

One rule above all: protect the mock exam time. It’s the hour that tells you whether you’re ready to book the real thing, or exactly which chapters to go back to.

That’s the whole point of a free weekend. Not to finish everything. To leave on Monday knowing exactly where you stand.

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Maratona do Rio fecha parceria com a TCS para tecnologia e IA. Incidente em meia maratona na Califórnia leva 27 corredores ao hospital com suspeita de envenenamento. World Athletics anuncia índices duríssimos para a maratona olímpica de Los Angeles 2028.
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Quarta-feira | 11 de novembro de 2026

A Maratona do Rio deu um passo importante para se consolidar no cenário internacional. A organização anunciou a Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) como sua nova parceira oficial de tecnologia e inteligência artificial. A TCS é uma gigante multinacional indiana, parte do Tata Group, e já é a parceira tecnológica de várias das principais maratonas do mundo, incluindo as Majors de Nova York, Londres e Sydney, além das maratonas de Amsterdã e Mumbai.

Essa parceria não se limita a expor a marca. A TCS é responsável por desenvolver os aplicativos oficiais dessas provas, implementar sistemas de telemetria, rastreamento de atletas em tempo real e aplicar soluções de análise de dados e inteligência artificial para otimizar a logística do evento, desde a largada até os serviços médicos e a transmissão para o público. Com isso, a expectativa é que a Maratona do Rio passe a contar com um padrão tecnológico de nível mundial, melhorando a experiência para corredores e espectadores. A iniciativa aproxima a prova carioca do sonho de se tornar uma Major, sendo a primeira maratona da América Latina a fechar um acordo com a empresa.

Incidente em meia maratona na Califórnia: 27 corredores são hospitalizados

Um incidente alarmante marcou uma meia maratona em Santa Bárbara, na Califórnia. Vinte e sete corredores foram hospitalizados após a prova, apresentando sintomas como alucinações e perda de memória recente. A principal suspeita é que a água de um dos postos de hidratação, localizado na altura da milha 11 (quilômetro 17), tenha sido contaminada com cetamina, um anestésico que pode causar efeitos alucinógenos.

Embora alguns tenham atribuído os casos ao calor, muitos atletas experientes estavam entre os afetados, e os sintomas relatados são atípicos para quadros de insolação. Médicos que atenderam os corredores afirmaram que o quadro clínico era típico de intoxicação por cetamina, a mesma substância que causou a morte do ator Matthew Perry. A polícia local está investigando o caso para confirmar se a água foi intencionalmente “envenenada”.

Índices para a maratona olímpica de Los Angeles 2028 ficam mais difíceis

A World Athletics divulgou os novos índices de qualificação para os Jogos Olímpicos de Los Angeles 2028, e os tempos para a maratona ficaram muito mais exigentes. Para garantir uma vaga direta, os homens precisarão correr abaixo de 2:05:00, enquanto as mulheres terão que fazer a marca de 2:22:20. Atualmente, o Brasil não possui atletas com esses tempos.

A qualificação, no entanto, não depende apenas do índice. Apenas 40% das 70 vagas (para cada gênero) devem ser preenchidas por atletas que atingirem a marca. As demais 60% serão distribuídas com base no ranking mundial da World Athletics. Outras formas de se classificar incluem ficar entre os cinco primeiros em uma maratona com selo Platinum ou, em último caso, ser indicado pelo comitê olímpico nacional, desde que o atleta tenha um tempo abaixo de 2:11 (homens) ou 2:29 (mulheres). A janela de qualificação começa em 1º de novembro de 2026 e vai até 30 de abril de 2028.
